articles.title: Day after Farooq dare, Srinagar MP Mehdi decides to quit Lok Sabha, NC over Article 370
articles.summary: India News: SRINAGAR: National Conference’s Srinagar MP Aga Ruhullah Mehdi announced Friday that he would resign from both Lok Sabha and the party, taking up patr.
articles.body: SRINAGAR: National Conference’s Srinagar MP Aga Ruhullah Mehdi announced Friday that he would resign from both Lok Sabha and the party, taking up patriarch Farooq Abdullah’s public dare to quit and contest an election on his own instead of criticising the brass repeatedly over its alleged dilution of the campaign for restoration of Article 370.Mehdi said he would formally send his resignation to LS Speaker Om Birla on Nov 3, coinciding with the 26th death anniversary of his father Aga Syed Mehdi, who was killed by terrorists.In a letter to Farooq, who remains NC president, Mehdi flagged what he sees as a dichotomy in the party’s stand on constitutional guarantees for the region. “I remember that you were the chief minister of the very assembly that passed the autonomy resolution. That, too, must have required courage. Why, then, has the mere mention of constitutional guarantees for Jammu & Kashmir now become so offensive that you felt compelled to publicly demand my resignation?”The MP described Article 370, struck off on Aug 5, 2019, as part of the decision to revoke J&K’s special status, as “shorthand for the struggle to restore the dignity, honour, constitutional guarantees and liberties” of Kashmiris.“Nearly 65% of J&K’s population is young, and their future is increasingly uncertain, with no jobs and opportunities. Our land is up for grabs. Our resources benefit everybody but us. Our religious rights, traditions and language face constant pressure,” Mehdi wrote.The MP has been increasingly critical of CM Omar Abdullah and NC for allegedly narrowing their fight to statehood and business rules for governance. Although a member of the party’s working committee, he hasn’t been part of crucial meetings.His rift with the party deepened after Dec 23, 2024, when he led a large student protest outside Omar’s Gupkar residence against the UT’s reservation policy. Omar engaged five student representatives in a long discussion but ignored Mehdi.Earlier this week, Farooq said Mehdi would not have won the parliamentary election without NC and accused him of trying to project himself as a powerful votary of Article 370 while being “on the wrong path”.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: I couldn't reach Yr Wyddfa's summit because of queue jumpers
articles.summary: Scores of visitors have climbed Yr Wyddfa this summer, with some facing long waits at the top.
articles.body:
When Helen Pacey and her family booked a trip on the Snowdon Mountain Railway, they were looking forward to touching the summit marker at the top of Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon.

But after spending 30 minutes waiting in a queue at the top of Wales' highest mountain, 58-year-old Helen ran out of time and had to get the return train back down.

"I've had both my hips replaced, so there was no way I could have gone up the rocky side of it," said Helen, from Hull in Yorkshire.

"Because people were pushing in, we missed out. That is not fair."

Scores of visitors have climbed Yr Wyddfa this summer, but there have been reports of people waiting more than an hour to reach the mountain's highest point, at 1,085m (3,560ft).

Earlier this week, we reported on arguments breaking out between queue-jumpers and those waiting in line at the top . Dozens of readers subsequently got in touch to share their views on the issue.

One of those who contacted us was Pacey, who hoped to touch the metal plate at the mountain's highest point alongside her husband, sister and brother-in-law.

But when Pacey and her family got off the train on 22 August, they were faced with a long queue.

"It was hectic," she said "There were people just pushing and shoving and running past us and climbing up the rocks to get up."

Pacey said the summit was so crowded that she was surprised nobody fell.

The group had only 30 minutes before their return train and they did not reach the trig point before they had to begin their descent.

"It was quite sad," she said. "It's really disappointing we didn't actually go right to the summit.

"But for me, it's not something I would do again, I just felt it was too dangerous up at the top with the amount of people shoving and pushing."

Pacey said the mountain was "for everybody", not just the "endurance runners and hikers".

"It's not fair that these people that are much fitter than others are just running up the rocks and getting to the top," she said.

Pacey said there should be an "authority figure" to help keep order, or a barrier telling people which way to go up and down the steps.

Serena Cain, 50, travelled from Norfolk to hike up the mountain with her partner for his 56th birthday.

She said when they got to the top and saw a long queue, it was "soul-destroying".

"I literally go to pieces in a queue," said Serena, who has ADHD and said she felt physical pain trying to stand still.

"It is very difficult for me, particularly when I'm exhausted and overstimulated."

Serena said when she saw other people avoiding the queue by climbing the rocks, she and her partner decided to do the same.

"We just didn't see what other option there was at that point, other than just not reaching the top, which would have been gutting," said Serena, adding that she had a birthday meal booked and needed to get back down in time for it.

Having climbed up the mountain's second hardest route, she added: "It was such a big achievement for us, because we're in our 50s, it's not a small feat."

But she recalled how one woman was "so cross with me" that "it ruined that moment completely for us".

"We didn't want to upset anyone, and we'd like to apologise if we did."

She said she understood why people waited in a queue, and thought there should be a sign at the beginning of the route to make people aware of the possibility.

James Munday, 21, from Loughborough, completed the Three Peaks challenge earlier this month and Yr Wyddfa was the last mountain he and his friends had to climb.

"It's a challenge where you hike up the three tallest mountains in the UK, which is Ben Nevis, Scarfell Pike, and Snowdon. The aim is to do it within 24 hours, including all of the driving. We managed to do it in 23 hours and 13 minutes."

Munday said he and his two friends were raising money for a hospice.

But their success depended on them making it up and down all three peaks within 24 hours, so when they spotted the queue at the summit of Yr Wyddfa, Munday said they had no intention of joining it.

"The queue started sort of towards the bottom of the steps that led up to the summit, but there was there was quite a few people not queuing and just climbing up the back, touching the top and then leaving straight away."

He said there were between 100 and 150 people queuing to get to the top.

As they were making their way to the top, he said a woman who was queuing "had a dig" and said "she'd been queuing for 40 minutes". Munday said they apologised and explained it was a timed Three Peaks challenge for charity.

"I feel like it was valid because obviously she doesn't know that we're doing the Three Peaks and that it's for charity. But I think if people understood... you have to do it under 24 hours, and if you're doing it for charity, I feel like people would understand a bit more."

Munday said he believed queuing was "Snowdon specific" due to how popular it is.

"And I think it's just what British people do, really, isn't it?"

He said if he had not been doing the challenge he would not have bothered going to the summit.

Munday said he had no issue with people queuing but "they either need to make it a rule that you must queue and signpost it, or police it... or have a queue and a sign that says Three Peaks climbers don't have to queue, please respect that".

Liam White said queues at the top of Yr Wyddfa had been an issue for years.

He said he and his friends climbed the mountain in 2023 and had to wait in a queue for more than 30 minutes to reach the summit.

"There were those that were just jumping the line, getting straight up to the peak and touching the old metal plate," he said.

"It's obviously a little bit frustrating because you're patiently waiting," he added.

He said his friend booed people as they cut past them.

The reason people queue is because of "the sheer volume of people" who are walking up the set pathways leading to the trig point, he said.

"When you've got a lot of people waiting to do something, you can't all rush out at the same time," he said. "If people start pushing and shoving, it's a bit of a risky place to do it. Because if someone slips, falls, they might not stop falling."

White said he did not think a warden would be good as he feared it could result in charges for hikers, but "maybe just a few signs to say 'be considerate'".

A spokesman for the Eryri National Park Authority previously said there were "no plans to intervene in a dispute over hikers queuing at the top of Yr Wyddfa".

"There are three quarters of a million people summitting annually, so queues are likely to be expected in peak times," the spokesman added.

He said the matter would be discussed at a meeting to mark the end of the season in the early autumn.

articles.title: Why space weather matters on Earth, and the team trying to protect us
articles.summary: The weather in space has the potential to impact our lives here on Earth in a fundamental way.
articles.body:
At the Met Office headquarters, the screens in one corner of the control centre are focussed on close up imagery of the Sun.

It is here that a space weather prediction team, one of only a small number worldwide, operates 24-hours a day, 365 days a year.

The weather in space has the potential to impact our lives here on Earth in a fundamental way. GPS, power grids and satellites are some of the vital technologies vulnerable to changes in the earth's magnetic field.

As a result, the Met Office has turned to Aberystwyth University researchers to help them improve their space weather forecasting abilities.

Space weather is mostly driven by activity on the Sun. Examples include solar flares, which are intense bursts of radiation.

The UK government has included severe space weather in its National Risk Register.

A 2025 estimate by Lloyds found that a severe space weather event could cost the world economy 2.4 trillion dollars ($2,400,000,000,000) over a five year period.

The Met Office has been working with key infrastructure operators since 2014 to try to keep us safe from those impacts, by producing forecasts using equipment on earth and satellites out in space.

Richard Stone, from the space forecasting team, said it allowed them "to diagnose anything that's happening on the Sun's surface, provide a forecast and alert the relevant users to be able to take mitigating actions".

Stone said the available technology was incredibly impressive, but still at an early stage.

"We've made great strides since 2014, but observations are still limited," he said.

Despite spotting an event on the Sun's surface around three days before it reaches Earth, there are no more sightings until it reaches satellites about one million miles away.

This gives scientists around one hour to more precisely predict its real effect on Earth and, if needed, warn partners of the mitigation needed to avoid disruption.

"It's like seeing a storm on the east coast of America and then not having any observations until it gets to Ireland," said Stone.

The agency has turned to a group of researchers, led by Aberystwyth University, to improve its forecasting abilities.

The project is being led by Professor Huw Morgan, who is Head of Space Physics at Aberystwyth University, working alongside Northumbria, Durham and Reading universities.

"This pre-warning is a huge mitigation of the danger posed by space weather," said Morgan.

"For example, it gives the National Grid an opportunity to prepare and avoid power cuts, or airlines can divert their flights from high latitude to safer lower latitudes.

"Compared to forecasting normal weather on Earth, space weather forecasting is really quite a developing field. I mean, it's yet to mature where we can give exact forecasts."

Scientists can already predict which years will be busiest for space weather events, with the Sun following an approximately 11-year activity cycle.

"We'll have some very quiet years, very little space weather, and then it peaks then, at the peak of the cycle then we can have a lot of space weather events, maybe several a day," said Morgan.

The Sun reached the peak of its activity cycle, known as the Solar Maximum, in 2024, which is why more of us saw the Northern Lights - another example of space weather.

But the forecast warnings provided to technology companies and infrastructure operators here on Earth means people have felt very little impact so, despite the Sun's increased activity.

An 1859 geomagnetic storm known as the Carrington Event is often considered to be the benchmark for a worst-case scenario here on Earth.

Named after English astronomer Richard Carrington, the effects were felt widely, with an aurora seen in the sky across much of the world and disruption to the telegraph network, which had only started operating commercially in the 1840s.

Stone said during the Carrington Event, "even telegraph wires were heard to hum and crackle, and they were able to run the telegraph poles without any electricity because the input was so high".

The concern now is that, without mitigation, a modern day Carrington Event would have significantly greater consequences due to our increasing reliance on technology.

And the impacts of space weather are not just a consideration for people on Earth.

In 1991, Helen Sharman became the first British person to travel into space on an eight-day mission to the Mir Space Station.

She was taught where to shelter if any space weather were to hit the space station.

Dr Sharman said during the mission she was affected by radiation from outside the solar system, called galactic cosmic rays.

"They come through the materials that spacecraft are made of," said Sharman.

"They come through astronauts' skin, and they're what we notice as astronauts because quite often we see little bright flashes of light on our retinas, as those particles come through the spacecraft, through our skin, through our eyes, and affect our vision in that way.

"The higher up you are as well, of course, the further away from the Earth's magnetic field, the more likely you are to not be protected by the Earth's magnetic field.

"So in low Earth orbit, by and large, we're fairly well protected. This is why, when astronauts go to the Moon, or possibly to Mars in the future, we really need to consider how we can protect them much better from radiation."

articles.title: Guernsey warning after wildfire the size of three football pitches breaks out
articles.summary: People have been urged to avoid the area and not start their own bonfires.
articles.body:
Islanders have been urged not to start bonfires after a wildfire the size of three football pitches broke out.

Guernsey Fire and Rescue Service was called to the blaze near Rue à Fresne in Castel earlier.

Guernsey Police advised people to avoid the area while firefighters extinguished the blaze.

Rory Quesnel, duty acting watch commander, said crews tackled the flames quickly, adding: "Everything is just so dry and I don't think people appreciate quite how fast something can get out of hand if you're doing a controlled burn."

He said a rapid intervention vehicle, further water carrier and rescue tender were sent to the scene.

The flames were extinguished later on Friday afternoon.

Firefighters then continued to dampen the area to prevent it from reigniting.

Quesnel said: "We would just like to urge people not to do controlled burns because we've been to so many incidents where a controlled burn has got out of hand.

"I think it really does surprise people when everything is tinder-dry, how quickly, with the wind that we get here, it can spread and just get out of control."

articles.title: Nilekani committee seeks public ideas to fix exams
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The high-powered task force set up by Centre to overhaul India’s public examination system opened a nationwide consultation on Friday, seek.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The high-powered task force set up by Centre to overhaul India’s public examination system opened a nationwide consultation on Friday, seeking suggestions from students, parents, teachers and other stakeholders on making high-stakes tests more secure, transparent and student-friendly.The panel, headed by Infosys co-founder and technology expert Nandan Nilekani, was announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi last month amid heightened scrutiny of the examination system following NEET-UG paper leak controversy and youth protests over alleged lapses in the test’s conduct.The announcement had come a day after Centre accepted the demands raised by the youth-led CJP, whose protests over NEET leak included calls for then education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation and withdrawal of FIRs against protesters. “The High-Powered Task Force (HPTF) on Reforms in Public Examinations wants to hear from students, parents, teachers — every citizen,” a senior official said on Friday.The task force’s mandate “to examine and recommend comprehensive reforms relating to conduct, security, design and governance of public examinations, including examinations conducted by National Testing Agency (NTA), the ministry of personnel said. HPTF, which seeks “to benefit from the experience, knowledge and perspectives of stakeholders”, said the suggestions may dwell on the conduct and security of public exams as well as the examination design and assessment methodology.Stakeholders may give inputs on better governance, accountability and institutional arrangements; as also systems to prevent, detect and redress examination malpractices, the ministry said. The public consultation will remain open till Sept 13, with citizens allowed to send suggestions through WhatsApp, a dedicated website, email and a toll-free number.Officials said the task force is examining reforms across the examination chain — from institutional processes and question-paper security to use of technology and strengthening of examination infrastructure.It will also look at measures to improve accessibility and inclusion, while factoring in student well-being during the examination process.“The objective is to develop a public examination system that is robust, secure, transparent, equitable and future-ready,” the official said. The exercise assumes significance after repeated controversies surrounding national-level entrance and eligibility examinations raised questions over paper security, examination management and the ability of testing agencies to respond quickly to irregularities. Apart from Nilekani, the task force includes former Isro chairperson S Somanath, former Intelligence bureau director Tapan Deka, IIT Madras director V Kamakoti, former education secretary Anita Karwal and logistics expert Amrit Lal Meena.The panel is expected to recommend both immediate safeguards and longer-term structural changes in the way public examinations are designed, administered and secured.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) disaster in Nepal Wednesday has renewed discussion on India's own strategy and preparedness to mitig.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) disaster in Nepal Wednesday has renewed discussion on India's own strategy and preparedness to mitigate such risk with the presence of approximately 200 high-risk glacial lakes in the Himalayan regions.According to govt's survey of these glacial lakes, Himalayan ranges are host to as many as 7,500 of them - with 10% in Sikkim and of which 25 are considered very high-risk. The study found 4,700 of these glacial lakes situated in Ganga river basin with a catchment area estimated at over 2.5 lakh sqkm, projecting a colossal scale of devastation a single breach could cause.India suffered one of the worst GLOF disasters in recent times when on Oct 3, 2023, glacial rocks of 14.7 cubic meter collapsed in South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim, close to midnight, "generating a 20-m high displacement wave", wiping out several hydro power assets and settlements on its way downstream.Krishna Vatsa, member of National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), said the Nepal event illustrates a new dimension of Himalayan disaster risk, though the precise sequence of events is still being scientifically established. "These are cascading hazards: an ice or rock failure can become a debris flow, create a temporary lake and then generate a flash flood. Such events can develop extremely rapidly and may provide very little warning time downstream.""India's National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme has marked 195 at-risk glacial lakes and follows five key priorities (assessment, monitoring, early warning, mitigation, community awareness). It needs to be speeded up and scaled up immediately as a priority for national security," said Syed Safi Ahsan Rizvi, an ex-NDMA member.As a response to the Sikkim disaster, Centre had set up a high-level coordination committee on GLOF disaster risk reduction. The initiative, spearheaded by PM's principal secretary PK Mishra, was tasked to host multi-agency deliberations and surveys of such lakes and identify the high-risk ones. Govt also allocated Rs 150 crore for the National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme for four Himalayan states having high-risk glacial lakes.The first meeting of the coordination committee on DRR was held in Nov 2024, when PM's principal secretary expressing his satisfaction on the group's "tri-focal lens: assessment, monitoring, and mitigation". The committee hosted regular meetings and received feedback, which were then formed as part of joint strategy between states and Centre. However, not much is known on follow up actions.Earlier, govt had claimed that multi-agency expeditions were conducted to assess all "A-category" lakes. The teams comprised scientists and officials from NDMA, Central Water Commission, Geological Survey of India, Centre for Development of Advance Computing, ITBP and the Army.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Built for $70,000 in 1976, this underground Missouri concrete home survived a deadly F4 tornado; 50 years later, it remains almost invisible from the road, hidden beneath a hillside
articles.summary: US News: When Tim and Monica open the front door of their home in Springfield, Missouri, there is little to suggest that a house is hidden beneath the hillside.
articles.body: When Tim and Monica open the front door of their home in Springfield, Missouri, there is little to suggest that a house is hidden beneath the hillside outside. Only a small corner of the structure is visible from the road, while much of the home disappears into the earth.The unusual underground residence was recently featured by architecture and design-focused YouTube channel Kirsten Dirksen, offering a look inside a home that was designed nearly five decades ago around the idea of becoming part of the landscape rather than sitting on top of it.Built in 1976 by architect and builder Dennis Spencer, the house occupies a sloping, north-facing site in Springfield. Instead of treating the difficult orientation and hillside as obstacles, Spencer incorporated them into the design, creating a concrete structure that is largely buried beneath earth and vegetation.For Tim and Monica, the unusual design has become an everyday reality. From the outside, even delivery drivers can struggle to identify the property as a house."There’s not a lot of concrete underground houses," they explain in the Kirsten Dirksen video, noting that the home is particularly unusual for Springfield.A house hidden inside the hillsideThe property was designed to blend into its surroundings. The roof is covered with roughly 14 to 15 inches of earth and vegetation, allowing grass and other natural elements to grow above the structure.Wildlife has seemingly accepted the house as part of the hillside. Turtles can be seen on the roof, birds inhabit the surrounding trees and a family of groundhogs has even made its home in the owners’ burn pile."The animals barely see the house. They think of it as kind of part of the hill," one of the homeowners says in the video.That was precisely the point of Spencer’s design.The house does not announce itself from the road. Instead, it nestles into the land, with only limited portions visible from outside. The result is a structure that appears less like a conventional residence and more like an extension of the hillside.Built with concrete and post-tensioned beamsDespite its seemingly natural appearance, the house is an extensively engineered concrete structure.It was constructed with cast-in-place concrete and post-tensioning technology. The roof uses a seven-inch concrete slab supported by upturned beams and was engineered to carry about 250 pounds per square foot.The construction technique involved allowing the concrete to cure before tensioning cables were installed. The cables compress the concrete, increasing its strength and durability.There are only three columns within the main interior space, allowing much of the home's interior to remain open and flexible.The roof was particularly important because it had to support the earth that would eventually be placed over the structure.The earth covering is not simply decorative. It forms part of the home's environmental strategy, helping insulate the interior and moderate temperatures throughout the year.The home was built for $70,000The unusual project was also remarkably inexpensive by today's standards.Spencer initially obtained a $50,000 loan to construct the house and later secured another $20,000, bringing the total cost to around $70,000.Securing financing was reportedly difficult because banks were unfamiliar with such an unconventional design."You present a set of plans for something so unique, the banks have a little hard time with it," the homeowners explain.Despite the challenges, Spencer completed the home and created a structure that would ultimately prove its worth in one of the most dangerous weather events to hit the neighbourhood.The 1990 tornado that tested the underground houseSpringfield lies in an area vulnerable to severe tornadoes, making the home's ability to withstand extreme weather a significant part of its story.In November 1990, an F4 tornado tore through the subdivision, destroying or severely damaging neighbouring properties and bringing down 41 mature trees around the underground house.The tornado passed directly over the property.While nearby conventional homes suffered devastating damage, the underground structure largely remained intact.The homeowners recall that the aftermath was more of a cleanup operation than a major repair project. The cars were destroyed, trees came down across the property and neighbouring houses were badly damaged, but the earth-covered concrete structure continued to provide shelter.The home's performance during the tornado demonstrated one of the fundamental principles behind its design: the earth itself could become a form of protection.‘The house did its work as a shelter’For Spencer, the home's relationship with the landscape was not simply an aesthetic decision. Its position within the hillside also gave it an inherent advantage during severe weather.One of the home's lowest and most deeply buried areas provided a particularly protected space during the tornado."You really do feel the sense of comfort, this safety, feeling like you're coming into the land but still having the shelter," the homeowners say.The house's concrete structure, combined with the earth berm surrounding it, effectively separated the living spaces from much of the destructive force experienced above ground.The tornado also provided an unintended real-world test of Spencer's approach to resilient architecture.An underground house that doesn't feel undergroundDespite being surrounded by earth, the interior is far removed from the dark, enclosed image often associated with underground homes.Tim recalls growing up exploring caves in Missouri and describes them as fascinating but sometimes dark and unsettling. This house, however, was designed to avoid that feeling.Natural light enters through skylights and large areas of glass. A ten-foot wall of east-facing glass helps connect the main living spaces to the landscape, while the layout creates repeated visual connections between the interior and exterior.The home includes a kitchen, dining area and living spaces with ceilings reaching around 10 feet in some areas.As the occupants move through the house, ceiling heights and corridors change, creating what the designers describe as moments of "compression and expansion." Narrower passages lead into larger rooms and courtyards, giving the interior a changing sense of scale.Even some of the deepest rooms remain visually connected to the outside through carefully positioned openings.The earth helps regulate the temperatureThe home's underground location also contributes to its energy efficiency.Concrete has significant thermal mass, allowing it to absorb heat and release it gradually as surrounding temperatures change. Combined with the earth surrounding the structure, this creates a stable indoor environment.The home's design takes advantage of this thermal inertia to reduce the impact of extreme outdoor temperatures.Although the property has modern mechanical systems, its occupants say the structure could remain comfortable even with those systems switched off under suitable conditions, relying on its relationship with the earth, ventilation and natural protection.The north-facing site presented a challenge for passive solar design because it limits exposure to the strongest southern winter sun. Spencer instead used the earth as a major component of the home's environmental strategy.A roof that becomes part of the landscapePerhaps the most striking feature is that the roof does not look like a conventional roof at all.With earth and vegetation covering the concrete structure, the roof becomes an extension of the hillside.In winter, the design takes on another role. Snow-covered slopes can make the home appear even more deeply embedded in the landscape, while the shape of the roof has also tempted neighbourhood children to use it for sledding."The land's just wrapping its arms around you," one of the homeowners says, describing the feeling of living beneath the hillside.The house's relationship with nature extends beyond its thermal performance. Wildlife treats the property as part of its habitat rather than as a conventional human structure.Nearly 50 years later, the experiment still worksSpencer's decision to build underground in 1976 may have seemed radical at the time, but nearly five decades later the house continues to demonstrate the potential of architecture that responds directly to its environment.It is difficult to spot from the street, difficult for delivery drivers to locate and almost indistinguishable from the surrounding landscape.But beneath the grass and earth is a carefully engineered concrete structure designed for strength, energy efficiency and resilience.Its survival of a devastating F4 tornado remains perhaps the clearest demonstration of the concept.While conventional houses around it were exposed to the full force of the storm, Spencer's home was protected by the very landscape into which he had built it.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Biggest deal in history’: Trump says US to control 65 billion barrels of Venezuela oil
articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump on Friday announced what he described as an agreement with Venezuela that would give the US control over 65 billion barrels .
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Friday announced what he described as an agreement with Venezuela that would give the US control over 65 billion barrels of the South American country's oil reserves.Trump said the deal was negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez. He announced the agreement in a social media post.“The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” Trump wrote.The announcement comes almost nine months after the US military, acting on Trump's orders, carried out an operation to capture Venezuela's President Nicolás Maduro. Maduro was taken to the US to face federal charges related to narcoterrorism and drug trafficking.The oil agreement also comes at a difficult time for Trump domestically, with high petrol prices putting pressure on his administration. The war in Iran has now reached its six-month mark with no clear end in sight, adding to concerns over energy supplies.The US has already been using its strategic petroleum reserves to help deal with energy pressures. The stockpile fell below 300 million barrels in early August, a drop of more than 100 million barrels since the beginning of 2026.Trump had discussed bringing US oil companies back to Venezuela shortly after Maduro was removed from power in January. He has also accused Venezuela of taking US oil after former President Hugo Chávez nationalised hundreds of foreign-owned assets, including those belonging to American oil companies.Venezuela has an estimated 303 billion barrels of crude oil reserves, making it one of the world's largest holders of oil. According to the US Energy Information Administration, this represents around 17% of global oil reserves.Much of Venezuela's oil is already mapped and known, meaning companies do not have to search extensively for new deposits. However, the country has struggled to turn those reserves into production because its oil infrastructure has deteriorated badly.As a result, Venezuela currently produces only around 1% of the world's oil despite holding such a large share of global reserves.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Nepal flood rescue hampered by mud and people trapped in tunnels
articles.summary: Nepal's military stepped up search and rescue operations after the devastating flash flood in the Himalayas, but faced major challenges including thick layer...
articles.body:
Nepal's military stepped up search and rescue operations after the devastating flash flood in the Himalayas, but faced major challenges including thick layers of mud and people trapped in mountain tunnels.

The mud was making it difficult for helicopters to land and take off in affected areas including Temure, Syabrubesi and Mailung, army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet said on Friday in Battar Bazar in Bagmati province, which borders Tibet.

Fourteen rescue helicopters were currently operating in the region and rescue efforts had been intensified, Basnet said. Nepal's disaster management authority said more than 4,400 people had been rescued by Friday evening.

The army has been using helicopters to evacuate people who were cut off from the outside world, bringing them to an army training camp in Battar Bazar. The army is primarily responsible for search and rescue operations during disasters in Nepal.

Tunnels in the mountainous region were another obstacle, Basnet said, with people being trapped inside. Only four people had been rescued from the tunnels by Friday morning, he said, adding that many more were thought to remain inside.

Video footage showed rescuers pulling two mud-covered workers alive from a tunnel at a hydropower plant. The men were carried on rescuers' backs to a helicopter.

It was difficult to say how long the rescue operations would continue, Basnet said.

Nepalese authorities said on Friday that 1,924 people were missing in the popular mountainous tourist region, including 517 foreigners. On the Chinese side of the border, in Tibet, 558 people were reported missing.

articles.title: Ancient Greek elites wore jewellery made from metal that fell from space; scientists identified meteorite iron in 3,000-year-old rings
articles.summary: Europe News: Long before iron smelting became widespread in Greece, some Bronze Age elites were already wearing jewellery made from iron that may have come from me.
articles.body: Long before iron smelting became widespread in Greece, some Bronze Age elites were already wearing jewellery made from iron that may have come from meteorites. A five-year study by Matthieu Gounelle of France's National Museum of Natural History and Eleni Mantzourani of the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens examined 105 Bronze Age and Early Iron Age artefacts from 33 archaeological sites held in 19 museums. Of the 105 objects, 91 were iron and were examined in detail using portable X-ray fluorescence. Thirteen iron objects, all rings or fragments of rings, contained significant amounts of nickel, a strong indicator of meteoritic iron. The researchers concluded that 9 of the rings were very likely made from meteoritic iron, another was quite likely to have been, while 3 require further investigation. The findings suggest that iron from meteorites was not simply a strange material encountered by chance, but a rare and valuable substance used for jewellery associated with powerful members of Minoan and Mycenaean society more than 3,000 years ago.How scientists identified meteorite iron in 13 ancient ringsThe study, titled Iron in Greece in the second millennium B.C.E., was published in the Journal of Archaeological Science. The researchers used portable X-ray fluorescence, or p-XRF, to examine the chemical composition of the objects without damaging them. This was particularly useful for fragile archaeological artefacts that could be difficult to remove from museum collections or transport to laboratories. Of the 91 iron objects analysed in detail, 78, or about 86%, contained no detectable nickel. These objects are consistent with iron produced through early smelting. The remaining 13 contained significant amounts of nickel. Because iron meteorites are naturally rich in nickel, the element provides an important chemical clue when researchers are trying to distinguish meteoritic iron from iron produced from terrestrial ores. The nickel concentrations in the rings varied considerably, ranging from about 1% to 50%, suggesting that the objects may not all have originated from the same meteorite. The researchers also note that nickel can be lost from archaeological iron during long-term burial and corrosion, meaning even relatively low concentrations can still provide evidence of an extraterrestrial origin.Why the meteoritic iron was used for ringsThe most striking pattern in the study was not simply the presence of nickel, but the type of objects in which it appeared. All 13 nickel-bearing objects were finger rings or fragments of rings. The wider collection included weapons, tools, jewellery and other iron objects, yet the evidence for meteoritic iron was concentrated entirely in the rings. Many of the rings were elaborate pieces featuring large, flat engraved surfaces and combinations of iron with other valuable metals such as gold, silver or bronze. Several came from richly furnished elite tombs in the Peloponnese, including sites such as Mycenae, Vapheio, Kakovatos, Aidonia and Dendra. The researchers argue that this pattern points to meteoritic iron having a special status. Rather than being used primarily as a practical material, it appears to have been selected for objects associated with wealth, prestige and social power. Eleni Mantzourani described the meteoritic iron as a very precious material used for objects of special value among high-status groups in Minoan and Mycenaean society.What the rings may reveal about Bronze Age tradeMeteorites containing large amounts of iron are relatively uncommon, and the researchers point out that meteorites are particularly scarce in Greece and Crete compared with some other regions of the eastern Mediterranean. That raises the possibility that meteoritic iron reached the Aegean through long-distance exchange networks. The researchers suggest Egypt as one possible source, given the established contacts between the Aegean and Egypt during the Bronze Age and the documented use of meteoritic iron in ancient Egypt. One of the best-known examples is the iron dagger found in the tomb of Tutankhamun, whose metal has been shown to have a meteoritic origin.The study does not, however, establish a specific trade route or prove that the Greek rings were made from Egyptian meteorites. The proposed connection remains a possibility that further research will need to test. Before this study, seven sites in the eastern Mediterranean had confirmed evidence of meteoritic iron. The researchers' work adds seven sites in Greece to that record, including Phaistos, Anemospilia, Mycenae, Vapheio, Kakovatos, Aidonia and Dendra.Why the meteorite-ring fashion disappeared around the 12th century BCEThe meteoritic iron rings appear to disappear from the archaeological record after the 12th century BCE, roughly coinciding with the upheavals associated with the Late Bronze Age collapse. That period saw the destruction or abandonment of Mycenaean palatial centres in southern Greece and major changes across the wider eastern Mediterranean. The researchers do not claim that the collapse directly caused the end of meteoritic iron jewellery. Instead, the timing suggests that changes to elite society and long-distance exchange networks may have played a role. The rings may simply have gone out of fashion, but the disappearance also occurred just as iron produced through terrestrial smelting was becoming increasingly important. That makes the rings particularly revealing. They capture a brief period when iron was still an unusual and prestigious material in the Aegean, long before it became the everyday metal that would define the coming Iron Age. For the people who wore these rings, the attraction may have been more than the metal's rarity. It was a material that had arrived from somewhere beyond the ordinary world a substance that had literally fallen from the sky and been transformed into jewellery for the most powerful people of Bronze Age Greece.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Landlady to 9/11 hijackers reveals their links to alleged Saudi spy
articles.summary: A woman who rented out homes to two al-Qaeda members speaks publicly for the first time - to the BBC.
articles.body:
Holly Ratchford still cannot believe that the man who moved into the residential complex she once managed would go on to be accused of involvement in the darkest day in recent US history.

"It's almost impossible for me to wrap my head around who he said he was, and who he really is. I still struggle with that," she tells the BBC.

The man, Omar al-Bayoumi - a Saudi in his early 40s - moved to the complex in San Diego, California, with his family in September 1999.

The new resident at number 152 Parkwood Apartments quickly became a regular at Ratchford's pool parties. "He was always so bubbly and smiling," she recalls, "and just very, very friendly."

A few months later, Bayoumi would introduce Ratchford to two apparently unassuming, "polite" men, who would also become her neighbours.

The pair would become infamous for hijacking American Airlines flight 77, and crashing it into the Pentagon, in the 9/11 attacks.

Ratchford has been haunted by her connection to these three men for the past 25 years. She feels she was taken in by Bayoumi from the start.

"Whenever I had parties he would come and be a part of the activities," she recalls, adding that his family would invite her in for food.

But Bayoumi, the one-time resident of 152 Parkwood, is now at the centre of the $1 trillion (£733bn) lawsuit brought against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by several thousand families of victims and as well as survivors of 9/11.

On 11 September 2001, four passenger aircraft were hijacked by 19 members of the Islamist extremist network, al-Qaeda. In addition to the crash at the Pentagon - the US military's headquarters near Washington DC - two planes were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, causing both buildings to collapse. A fourth crashed in a field in Pennsylvania, following resistance from passengers on board.

In all, almost 3,000 people were killed, including about 300 firefighters and other emergency workers at the World Trade Center.

Bayoumi is alleged to have facilitated the 9/11 plot through the support he provided for the first two hijackers to arrive in the US - Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar - who lived at Parkwood for several months prior to the attacks.

The federal judge in the 9/11 families' lawsuit in New York found a year ago that the evidence created "a reasonable inference" that Bayoumi and a Saudi diplomat based in the US had been "co-ordinating with the Saudi government when providing assistance to the hijackers".

The judge's ruling has allowed the families' case to move forward. Saudi Arabia is appealing it and, together with Bayoumi, has always denied the allegations.

Ever since the attacks, Bayoumi has been the subject of reporting and speculation.

Ratchford - who saw him interacting with the hijackers and witnessed him providing a crucial act of support for them - has given a sealed declaration to the New York court.

But she has never spoken publicly about what she saw.

After unwittingly becoming embroiled in the investigation into what the US government has described as "the most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history", she moved about as far from humanity as you can get in the United States.

I tracked her down to the high desert in the western US - rattlesnake country. She told me she avoided the news, and definitely did not speak to journalists. But, to my surprise, she agreed to talk.

Her interview with me casts doubt on the version of events Bayoumi has told police, the FBI and the New York court, and features in the BBC Radio 4 podcast, Intrigue: A 9/11 Story , and an upcoming BBC Panorama, 9/11: The Saudi Connection .

In early 1999, Ratchford landed on her feet. Life before then had been untethered - she had moved around, been married, pregnant and divorced before she was 21. But now, aged 27, she had a job she loved and a home.

As the new property manager of Parkwood Apartments, a squat complex of 175 low-rise apartments and townhouses in the San Diego suburbs, she says she excelled. Properties were never empty for long. But it was not the paperwork, nor the healthy pay check, that made the job a dream, it was the people.

Ratchford not only worked at Parkwood, she lived there too. Her clients were also her neighbours. And many were more than that - she says they became her friends.

"I always told my staff: 'You make them feel like this is their home, and they'll stay,'" she recalls.

As Ratchford made her mark at Parkwood, she was happy and secure in the world she had built - a world in which she knew everyone and everything.

Then, things fell apart in a dramatic and unexpected way.

Omar al-Bayoumi moved into Parkwood claiming to be a mature student.

"I knew he was going to school. I'm not sure, other than that, what he did," Ratchford says.

More than two decades later, declassified FBI documents and court filings would reveal that Bayoumi's studies had, in effect, come to a halt in 1998. He was spending much more time organising religious activities in the Muslim community, which he often videotaped.

His constant filming, and his inquiring questions, aroused suspicions.

"It was a general consensus of people in the San Diego Muslim community that Bayoumi was an operative of the Saudi intelligence service," Richard Lambert, who led the city's FBI office investigation after 9/11, tells me.

But it was not Ratchford's business to pry. What mattered to her was whether he could pay the rent. And he could.

The FBI would later discover he was being paid about $90,000 (£55,600 at the time) a year.

Bayoumi presented himself as an ordinary family man.

The Bayoumi who Ratchford saw was captured on his never-before-broadcast home movies - throwing a ball around with his family by the Parkwood pool, laughing when it drifted into the water.

Another video reveals him on an excursion to Las Vegas with his family. Wearing a floral shirt, he points out the rollercoaster by the New York, New York hotel casino.

"I bought into everything that he told me. I really thought that's how he was," Ratchford says.

But that version of Bayoumi is at odds with the man who emerges from other videos.

In summer 1999, Bayoumi filmed the United States Capitol in Washington DC from different angles, noting a "plan", and turning the camera on himself to deliver a reporter-style commentary.

The 9/11 families' lawyers allege he was surveilling the building as a potential target for the attacks. The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia maintains it is a tourist video.

In his August 2025 judgement, the New York judge found that "all the Court can conclude" from the video is that Bayoumi "visited Washington DC and that he filmed the city".

On 3 February 2000, Bayoumi brought two young men into Ratchford's San Diego rental office. In an obvious hurry, she says, he perched on the filing cabinet as he told her that the two men were from his mosque and were staying with him while they looked for a place to rent.

"There was absolutely nothing unusual about them. They were nice, they were polite," she recalls.

The two men spoke no English, but Bayoumi took charge. Ratchford says he asked her what the two men would need to show in order to qualify for a Parkwood apartment.

"They didn't meet the income criteria at all, or the bank account. They had none of that," she tells me.

But the two men did have several thousand dollars in cash. Bank records show that, the following day, Bayoumi took them to the nearest bank and helped them open an account.

Back at Ratchford's office on the third day, he figured a way around the problematic income criterion. He would co-sign their lease - becoming the legal guarantor for their apartment.

The rental agreement shows Bayoumi's multiple signatures. He was their guarantor, their friend, their emergency contact, and his Parkwood home was listed as their current address.

Without further delay, the two men moved into number 150, a one-bed apartment just a few doors down from Bayoumi's poolside townhouse.

The two men Bayoumi was assuming legal responsibility for - Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar - would become 9/11 hijackers.

Holly saw the pair repeatedly in the following few months.

"I would have cookies and tea with them. It wasn't like they were just someone that came into the office and rented from us," she says.

Hazmi and Mihdhar stayed in their apartment until the end of May that year, and then moved out. Ratchford thought no more about it.

Sixteen months later, as America reeled in shock and grief in the days following the 9/11 attacks, she says a woman called asking her for a rental reference for them. Without thinking, she rattled off their details.

But the woman was not a property agent - she was a reporter.

Her next question shook Ratchford: "Did you know that they were two of the terrorists that flew their plane into the Pentagon?"

On 14 September 2001, two special agents interviewed Ratchford in her Parkwood office.

She gave them Bayoumi's guarantor form, triggering an investigation into the man they would come to see as the main facilitator of the two hijackers' lives in San Diego.

Richard Lambert, now retired from the FBI and working as a consultant to the 9/11 lawsuit families, says "as we began to identify the hijackers' associates, what became clear is that there was a network headed up by Omar al-Bayoumi".

The FBI found that Bayoumi's contacts had helped Hazmi and Mihdhar obtain California driver's licences, apply to flight schools, receive Middle Eastern wire transfers, and even arrange dental treatment.

The FBI agents wanted to interview Bayoumi. They traced him more than 5,000 miles (8,000km) to the UK, to Birmingham, where he had moved just before 9/11.

On 21 September 2001, he was arrested by the Metropolitan Police's anti-terror branch and detectives began questioning him.

Seeming unflustered, and at times indignant, Bayoumi initially denied knowing any of the hijackers.

He said he had often helped people find accommodation but, when detectives pressed him, said he could not remember the names of anyone for whom he had guaranteed an apartment.

A day later, he said he remembered helping two individuals, "Nawaf" and "Khalid" - the first names of Hazmi and Mihdhar.

He admitted they were the only two people to whom he had given this level of support.

Bayoumi claimed he had met the pair in Los Angeles, after briefly overhearing them speaking Arabic in a restaurant. He said he had told them that if they ever went to San Diego, he could help them.

The next day, he told the British detectives, the men had shown up at his local mosque in San Diego saying they needed a place to live. He had then driven them back to Parkwood to see Ratchford about finding them an apartment.

After Hazmi and Mihdhar had moved in, Bayoumi said he had avoided them. He said he had left town, and that when he returned, he found they had moved on.

In his account, Bayoumi's association with the future hijackers was fleeting. But his story does not match Ratchford's version of events.

"I know that's what he said, and I know that's bullshit," she says.

Before he brought the hijackers to her office, Ratchford says Bayoumi had asked her several times about finding an apartment for two people.

"I would tell him what would be available and he'd be like, 'oh no, no, I want that one'," she says. "He wanted something near him, and he was hoping for the least expensive place."

She also contradicts Bayoumi's claim that he hardly saw the hijackers after he secured their apartment, explaining that she had seen them together over the weeks that followed. On one occasion, the three of them had come to her office for tea and cookies.

"It's not like he just found them an apartment and never talked to them again," she says, adding that the three men "were definitely friendly".

Ratchford also told the FBI that when the hijackers had fallen behind with paying their rent, Bayoumi had paid it.

The Met Police held Bayoumi for seven days - the maximum at the time. The US Department of Justice (DOJ) decided not to extradite him to face charges.

On 28 September 2001, Bayoumi was released.

"I can't believe he got away," she says.

The FBI continued to build a case against him, however.

San Diego agents discovered that two companies linked to the Saudi Ministry of Defence were providing Bayoumi with his $90,000 pay, but that he never went to work and accrued "outrageous" expenses.

His pay more than doubled just after the two hijackers' arrival in San Diego, agents found, and fell again after they left the US west coast.

Meanwhile, agents from the New York FBI office combed through a trove of documents received from the Met Police, following the search of Bayoumi's properties in Birmingham, the BBC has learned.

The FBI uncovered letters to a Saudi government-linked charity with direct ties to al-Qaeda, materials which they assessed could "demonstrate Omar al-Bayoumi's anti-American sentiments and beliefs", and writings by Bayoumi himself which they determined "can be interpreted as jihadist".

But none of this led to an indictment or prosecution.

The DOJ told the BBC it was unable to comment on matters and decisions from 25 years ago, involving staff who no longer worked there.

9/11: What happened and how many people died in September 11 attacks?

Bayoumi left the UK for Saudi Arabia in August 2002.

Two years later, he was, in effect, cleared when the US's 9/11 Commission - the independent inquiry into the attacks - concluded he was "obliging and gregarious" and "an unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists". The FBI had not shown the Commission all the evidence it had gathered - and declined to comment when the BBC asked about this.

Meanwhile, the 9/11 families had started their attempts to pursue him through the courts, adding him as a defendant to their $1tn suit against various individuals, companies and governments for allegedly supporting al-Qaeda.

For years, the families campaigned for the FBI's investigation to be declassified. The wait was agonisingly slow, but since 2018 tens of thousands of pages of documents have been released to the New York court and via a presidential order signed by Joe Biden - including the FBI's interviews with Holly Ratchford.

In August last year, having considered the entire body of evidence, the judge in the 9/11 families' legal case said the evidence did not support the conclusion that Bayoumi had been "just an innocent participant".

Judge George B Daniels also noted later in his judgement that there was "a reasonable inference that all the apartment-related assistance he [Bayoumi] provided for the hijackers was not just acts of a good Samaritan, but rather that he was following" instructions from the Saudi government.

Saudi Arabia denies any involvement in 9/11 and has consistently argued that Omar al-Bayoumi was not a Saudi agent and did not have any involvement or foreknowledge of the attacks. It maintains that, under US law, it has sovereign immunity - official exemption of a ruler or state from certain types of civil suit and criminal prosecution - and that the case should be struck out.

The case is now with the US Court of Appeal, which will hear oral arguments in October.

9/11 was a catastrophe that wrought personal trauma on tens of thousands of people - the families of the victims, the survivors, first responders and witnesses.

For Holly Ratchford, all the certainties and securities of her years at Parkwood came to an abrupt end.

"I know a lot of peoples' lives changed immediately during 9/11. For me, within a week or two, my life, my ideals, my beliefs, everything changed so quickly. It was like a flip of a switch," she says.

"I felt so stupid. I trusted and I cared about people that did bad things. I don't ever want to be as blindsided as I was by them not being who they said they were."

Soon after 9/11, Ratchford quit Parkwood, property management, and the big city.

She moved first to the beach, then to a reservation, and later, to the middle of nowhere - all in an effort to escape the feeling she was being tricked.

Ratchford kept to herself, she tells me, interacting only with people she absolutely trusted.

"9/11 made me afraid of people," she says.

"Now I just prefer to be away from people that might be lying about who they are. You can't keep a secret when you live in a small town and that makes me feel more safe. I like being in a place where I can trust people."

But even as she has sought to escape further and further from the outside world, she is haunted by questions about what happened at Parkwood.

"Part of me wonders if there's something I could have done if I was more strict," she says.

articles.title: How 'Book Queen' Dolly Parton inspired millions of children with gift of reading
articles.summary: Families across the globe share how free books from Parton's Imagination Library helped their children.
articles.body:
One child in Denver called her "The Book Queen".

Another in Alabama calls her "Ms Dolly".

Across the globe in Australia, a toddler with speech delays delighted her family with her first word - "orange" - after she and her twin sister received a free book in the post about colours. It came from Imagination Library, the literacy programme begun by late global superstar Dolly Parton.

Parton, who died this week aged 80, launched the philanthropic effort in 1995 to honour her father - whose difficult Appalachian upbringing never allowed him to finish school or learn to read and write.

"He was the smartest man I have ever known, but I know in my heart his inability to read probably kept him from fulfilling all of his dreams," wrote Parton in an open letter on Imagination Library's website.

"Inspiring kids to love to read became my mission."

Imagination Library sends one free book a month to children from birth to age five. It first launched in Tennessee's Sevier County, where Parton grew up, before expanding across the US in 2000. The programme, which partners with local organisations, launched in Canada in 2006, the UK the following year, then Australia in 2013 and Ireland in 2019.

By 2025, as Imagination Library celebrated its 30th anniversary, it had distributed more than 300m books - equating to one book mailed every 78 seconds, according to the organisation.

And for the families in receipt of the storybooks, the impact has been invaluable.

Tennessee governor plans to name Nashville airport after Dolly Parton

"It just blows my mind that it's readily available for every family that lives in my borough," said London mother-of-two Harriet Anscombe, whose four-year-old daughter has been receiving Imagination Library books since she was three months old.

The free books helped Anscombe establish a reading-focused nighttime routine.

"I think that, if I didn't get those books, maybe I wouldn't have started doing bedtime stories till she was two - but because we were getting them so early, it embedded story time into our routine from when she was just a couple of months old," Anscombe said. "She probably doesn't remember a time when we weren't reading stories."

Imagination Library became part of the family routine for Ciara Fernandez Faber, too, after she signed up her son about eight years ago in Colorado. His favourite book for years was one written by Parton herself: I Am A Rainbow.

"We read it almost every night, and I never got tired of reading it to him," said Faber, 42.

"It's a book about different emotions, and so we would act out the different emotions, the different faces," she said. "At the back of the book, there's a little excerpt by Dolly talking about how everybody has a rainbow of feelings, and we would read that - and he would always point to her picture and say, 'There's the Book Queen.'"

Families like Faber's repeatedly remarked on how well curated the books were - detailing how topics helped their children not just with reading, but also with social and emotional development.

"There were themes that were addressed in a lot of the books that would have really helped us navigate issues," said Helen Cashell, of Dublin, Ireland.

She signed up both of her children, now aged seven and five, for the scheme. "Whether it was same-sex families or just different types of families, things about bravery, courage, bullying, things about different identities."

Author Selina Brown, whose book My Rice Is Best was selected for distribution through Imagination Library, noted how the plotline features a black protagonist.

The programme also helps promote authors like herself; because of the selection, it "means 14,000 copies of my book have been sent to children in the UK".

"To choose between gas, electric, food or a book, you're going to choose a core need - but with the Dolly Parton Imagination Library, you don't have to do that," she said.

In inner-city Sydney, Australia, first-time mum Paige Stewart was astounded as she watched her children's progress with the programme.

Her twin girls, now four, "had a speech delay and some learning difficulties" - but Stewart noticed a change after just the second book.

"Not only did they learn their colours from that book… it kind of set the tone for them speaking and their joy for books."

She's become a vocal advocate for the programme, telling others: "It's so helpful, honestly."

Alabama grandmother Kristina Hadley also promotes the programme to friends and family - even incorporating Imagination Library into baby gifts.

"I'll pull up the Imagination books website, and I'll print that, and I'll put it in a picture frame, and I'll get little newborn books and stuff like that, and I'll put it with that for like a suggestion for new mothers," said Hadley, 53.

She signed up her nearly three-year-old granddaughter, Eillie Elaine, "before she was actually born". Now the child has her own bookshelf in their shared household - "and one whole shelf is for her Dolly books".

"She likes to go to go to the mailbox, and she's like, 'Ms Dolly! Ms Dolly!' and I'm like, 'Well, let's go see if Ms Dolly sent you a book!'"

A lifelong Parton fan, Hadley chokes up while detailing how she was at work when a friend texted to say the singer had died.

Imagination Library, she says, "is going to keep her memory going with the younger generation, and I hope and I pray that this is something that goes on for years and years and years."

It's a legacy that Parton built quietly in the background as she presided over pop culture for more than six decades.

"The biggest thing that I like is the fact that she didn't do anything for recognition," said Geoff Blacklin, 67, of Manitoba, Canada.

He and his wife signed up their grandchildren for Imagination Library after a local doctor brought the programme to their region.

"She gave families more than books," Blacklin said. "She gave children a love of reading, precious moments with loved ones, and opportunities to learn and dream."

Such family stories and gratitude would undoubtedly have been music to Parton's ears; the expansion of the programme was truly a realisation of her own dream.

"In the beginning, my hope was simply to inspire the children in my home county, but here we are today with a worldwide programme that gives a book a month to well over 3 million children," she wrote on the Imagination Library site - also taking care to thank the partners "who have embraced my dream and made it their own".

At the centre of it, always, was her love for children - and her love for her father.

"Before he passed away, my Daddy told me the Imagination Library was probably the most important thing I had ever done," Parton wrote.

"I can't tell you how much that meant to me, because I created the Imagination Library as a tribute to my Daddy."

articles.title: Mountain of fridges is building, warns national council body
articles.summary: This year's multiple heat waves have increased the numbers of fridges and freezers breaking down.
articles.body:
A mountain of broken fridges is building up in waste centres across England and Wales, the Local Government Association (LGA) has warned.

This year's multiple heat waves have increased the numbers of white goods such as fridges and freezers breaking down and needing to be scrapped at specialist sites.

Dozens of councils have been forced to stop collections of white goods due to a major backlog, which has built up due to a national shortage of specialists needed to safely process the appliances.

Earlier this month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the latest crackdown on illegal waste dumps - and the LGA is now calling on the government to take urgent action on dealing with white goods too.

LGA Neighbourhoods committee chair Councillor Arooj Shah called on the government to force white goods companies to pick up the burden, help councils with the cost of extra storage, and prevent the same problems recurring in future.

"The backlog of defunct white goods is getting bigger by the day – they're at risk of becoming a mountain," he said.

"It is not right that residents who are trying to do the right thing can't take old or broken appliances to their local recycling centre due to failures elsewhere in the system."

Councils from Bradford to Gloucestershire , Durham and Nottingham are among 26 to have suspended fridge collections this month.

A Department for Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) spokesman acknowledged the capacity issues and said short-term storage was being set up.

He said: "Our priority is to minimise disruption to household collection or proper disposal of fridges and other cooling equipment, and we are pushing producers of these items to take all necessary steps to achieve this and resolve any collection delays."

Fridges and freezers require specialist dismantling due to the gases they contain, which can be harmful to the environment if not disposed of safely, but three of the UK's 10 full-scale processing plants have closed in the last 12 months.

The three closures - due to a fire, bankruptcy and a change of use - have been compounded by this year's heat waves, as the remaining plants cannot operate above 30 degrees Celsius.

Industry body the Environmental Services Association said this year's closures had ended up "knocking out capacity suddenly" and executive director Jacob Hayler said:

"The result is that capacity is now constrained nationally until facilities can be brought back online or new capacity is permitted and developed."

Fridges from the UK are now being exported to Europe to meet demand, with only one more UK processing plant due to open next year.

Funding for processing relies on the companies that make white goods, who must register with a compliance scheme and tell them how many tonnes of appliances they sell per year, then the scheme collects the same weight of material and coordinates disposal.

The recycling of white goods is handled by 15 producer compliance schemes, who coordinate the collection, recycling and disposal of units from the UK, increasingly via European processing plants.

The largest of these compliance schemes is not-for-profit Ecogenesys, which works with about 85 councils in the UK, and is supporting the development of new UK fridge processing infrastructure.

Ecogenesys chief executive Graeme Milne said European processing plants would provide a temporary stop-gap but the UK needed more processing capacity in the long-term, adding: "The UK fridge recycling sector has faced exceptional pressures this summer, but we expect the situation to begin to ease as the seasonal peak passes."

John Redmayne, the managing director of another compliance scheme, the European Recycling Platform, said the UK is "facing a genuine capacity crunch" on recycling old fridges, adding the industry consensus "points to a six to twelve month recovery".

The bottleneck in the disposal of white goods has led to fears of increased flytipping as the government starts a major crackdown on illegal waste dumps.

Country Land and Business Association president Gavin Lane said finding a flytipped fridge dumped in a field was "a farmer's nightmare".

"It can cause hours of disruption, stress, and clean-up bills running into the thousands," he said, calling on the government to get the system working.

One of England's 11 so-called illegal "super sites", the Kidlington dump of about 22,000 tonnes of waste in Oxfordshire has been cleaned up this week - but at a cost of £6m to the public purse.

The government is now targeting organised crime gangs, who are behind hundreds of illegal dumps are operating across England, to seize assets bought with the proceeds of crime, as well as hiking fines from £300 to £5,000.

articles.title: Close race as Iceland votes on whether to restart talks on joining EU
articles.summary: Turbulent international affairs have brought the vote forward, but the campaign has focused more on Iceland's vital fishing industry.
articles.body:
Icelanders are voting in a referendum to decide whether to resume talks on joining the European Union, 13 years after they were broken off.

In an indication of how tight the result is expected to be, the latest opinion poll put the No campaign in the lead with 51.6%. An earlier poll had put the Yes campaign ahead.

Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government had already intended to hold a referendum, but turbulent international affairs prompted her to bring it forward.

But the debate was fought less over Nato member Iceland's security concerns than over its vital fishing industry and sovereignty.

Voting is due to go on from 09:00 to 22:00 GMT on Saturday and the result is expected in the early hours of Sunday.

Iceland has a population of under 400,000. More than one in five voters had already cast their ballots in early voting before Saturday, according to Iceland's public broadcaster RUV.

The question on the ballot is : "Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?"

Although Iceland is already part of the EU's single market and Schengen border-free zone as part of the European Economic Area, EU membership would bring it into the customs union and eventually the euro.

Iceland's application to join the EU was already well advanced when it put talks on hold in 2013, and European Commission officials have indicated that talks could be finalised in one or two years. Of the 35 so-called chapters of talks ranging from fisheries and economic policy to freedom of speech and free movement of goods, 27 had begun and 11 of them were provisionally complete .

A Yes vote would not be a final decision on joining the EU. It would mean backing a move towards an accession agreement. Any deal would then have to be approved by a second referendum, as well by parliament, and the constitution would have to be amended. The EU's 27 member states would also have to sign it off.

One Yes-campaign group, "Yes to See", says Icelanders should at least see what deal they can get, so they have all the information before a final decision.

Equally, a No vote would not rule out the chance of Iceland resuming talks in the future.

Sovereignty has been a crucial issue in the pre-referendum debate. Iceland fought hard to become fully independent from Denmark in 1944, and its fishing and marine industries make up almost 40% of exports.

No campaigners fear losing control over Iceland's prized fishing grounds under the EU's Common Fisheries Policy and they have vowed never to share their waters with anyone. Brussels has indicated Iceland could earn some kind of exemption, but it is considered potentially the biggest obstacle to any agreement.

Many Icelanders remember the so-called Cod Wars with the UK that Iceland won in the 1970s. And fisheries was always the issue that stopped Iceland joining the EU before.

However, in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of Iceland's banking system, Reykjavik moved to start accession talks in 2009, only to bring them to a halt in 2013.

Iceland is now one of Europe's most affluent nations and Eirikur Bergmann, professor of politics at Bifröst University, told the BBC that "many people attribute this to Iceland's independence".

One Icelandic trade union survey suggested this year that the country was more expensive than the next 10 most expensive countries in the world.

Although it has the fifth highest GDP (economic output) per capita in the world, interest rates are stubbornly high at 8% and inflation has climbed to 5.6%.

Yes campaigners argue that the economic benefits of the EU would help bring the rates down.

Iceland may be a founder member of Nato but it has no military and relies on its allies for defence.

A bilateral US defence agreement has been in place since 1951 and the No campaign has said Iceland's security rests on both Nato and the US and EU membership is not a substitute for Nato.

Iceland has been a strong supporter of Ukraine during Russia's full-scale invasion and officials have viewed Russia's increased maritime manoeuvres near the island with alarm.

However, there has also been concern at US President Donald Trump's expressed interest in taking over Greenland, and the fact that he has confused it with Iceland has caused alarm.

This year the EU and Iceland signed a security and defence partnership, and EU officials said the EU "offers an anchor in a community of values, prosperity and security".

Ahead of the referendum, the two sides held a televised debate where the Yes campaign team was headed by Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir and the No campaign was led by Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir, chair of the opposition Independence Party.

Kristrún told the audience that Iceland was already well integrated in the European Union, and becoming a member would be "one of the biggest risk-reducing steps we can take".

She also made clear that a Yes vote did not necessarily mean that Iceland would join, and that if there was a No vote, the result would be respected.

Guðrún, meanwhile, stressed that the vote was not about whether Iceland should work well with Europe: "We already do, and we want that to continue."

Instead, she portrayed the referendum as a vote on whether Icelanders wanted to hand "decision-making powers" to Brussels on fisheries, agriculture and their natural resources.

Although geopolitics kick-started the government's decision to push for a return to EU talks, there has been little discussion of it during the campaign.

"It's lower on the agenda than many would think," says Hallgrimur Oddsson, director of EU-Iceland think-tank European Currents.

articles.title: Report: Tanker pays record $5.3m to transit Panama Canal
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A tanker carrying liquefied petroleum gas has paid $5.3 million for priority passage through the Panama Canal ahead of El Nino-related restrictions, t.
articles.body: A tanker carrying liquefied petroleum gas has paid $5.3 million for priority passage through the Panama Canal ahead of El Nino-related restrictions, the waterway’s deputy administrator, Ilya Espino de Marotta, said Thursday. South Korean company SK Gas paid the record sum for the G Spirit to transit the shipping lane on Sept 1, two days before canal authorities reduce the number of transits due to the El Nino weather phenomenon, Bloomberg reported.Panama on Tuesday became the latest Central American country to declare an emergency over El Nino, which has caused dwindling water levels in the canal due to a severe droug­ht across the region. El Nino is a weather pattern that raises surface temperatures in the ce­ntral and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, generating global cha­n­g­es in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions.Ships transiting the Panama Canal book their passage well in advance, and ships without bookings wait an average of five days to get through, but there is an auction where last-minute transits can be purchased. The Panama Canal Authority said in a statement that the average auction price between Oct 2025 and Feb 2026 was around $55,000. But in April, a vessel carrying liquefied natural gas paid $4 million to skip the line and avoid a wait to pass through the canal as the war in West Asia boosted demand to move vital cargo via the waterway.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
