articles.title: Chinese rescuers manage to reach core disaster zone 50 hrs after flood
articles.summary: China News: More than 50 hours after Wednesday’s flash flood, Chinese professional rescuers reached the core disaster zone around Gyirong dry port on Nepal-Tibet .
articles.body: More than 50 hours after Wednesday’s flash flood, Chinese professional rescuers reached the core disaster zone around Gyirong dry port on Nepal-Tibet border for the first time on Friday afternoon, using inflatable boats, mountain trails, ropes and heavy-lift drones to bypass obliterated roads. Twenty-one firefighters — six from Tibet and 15 from Sichuan — along with a search dog reached the border-gate area around 4.30pm, hours after an overflowing barrier lake upstream forced rescuers to withdraw to safer ground.The breakthrough came after rescuers adopted what China’s national fire and rescue administration described as a “water, land and air” operation: inflatable boats pushed through waterways, teams crossed mountains on foot, and drones surveyed the destruction and carried equipment and supplies into areas vehicles could no longer reach.Chinese Premier Li Qiang travelled to Gyirong County on Thursday after being dispatched by President Xi Jinping, inspected the disaster zone, met rescuers and visited temporary shelters in the accessible parts of the disaster zone. “As long as there is a glimmer of hope, every effort should be made,” Li said.By Friday evening, China had mobilised 681 national fire and rescue personnel and 113 vehicles to Gyirong, including teams from Tibet and Sichuan, and sent 6,612 pieces or sets of rescue and support equipment.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Why sweetcorn treats are the latest 'swavoury' UK food trend
articles.summary: From lattes to pastries, UK foodies are embracing the humble sweetcorn as more than a pizza topping.
articles.body:
That's according to Crystelle Pereira, a cook and former Great British Bake Off finalist known for her wacky flavour combinations.

While sweetcorn is already a staple in South East Asian and Latin American puddings, it has largely been relegated to sandwich fillings and pizza toppings in the UK. But that could all be changing.

In recent weeks, the vegetable has been popping up all over social media in sweet treat form - as an ingredient in everything from cookies and ice cream to cheesecake.

Food trend forecasters say sweetcorn is starting to appear in "some exciting and unexpected guises" on the UK food scene.

It is all part of a wider food trend involving the combination of sweet and savoury flavours we wouldn't traditionally put together, sometimes called the "swavoury" movement, Shokofeh Hejazi of food trend agency thefoodpeople says.

Other examples include combinations like purple sweet potato ice cream, cheesecake with carrot compote, or chocolate bars loaded with salty potato chips.

Both sweetcorn's flavour profile and ability to be blended into a creamy texture makes it a great fit for the trend, says Hejazi.

Pereira says sweetcorn in desserts and drinks is "very slowly easing its way" into the UK food scene.

And she's excited: "I genuinely really think sweetcorn and desserts is just the best thing in the world.

"We've been so used to having sweetcorn in tuna and sweetcorn, we just think it's a savoury ingredient," she says. "But… it's so, so sweet."

Pereira had an "epiphany" when she saw the ingredient being used in sweets on holiday in Thailand last year, where it's common to see sweetcorn used in everything from custard tarts to jellies and ice creams.

Hoping to inspire her UK followers to experiment with the vegetable, she made a sweetcorn latte inspired by a frappé drink she'd had on her trip, using coconut milk, blended sweetcorn and espresso.

"I wanted to show people that it works," she tells me, explaining she thought sweetcorn's similarity to condensed milk would make the combination "more palatable" to a sweetcorn drink novice.

​​Lisa Harris, co-founder of food consultancy Harris & Hayes, says growing interest in sweetcorn is also partly down to the UK's "unstoppable" appetite for South Korean food , which is "changing how we eat".

Pereira has continued to champion corn, recently making a Brazilian lemonade - which uses limes instead of lemons - and pairing it with corn milk.

But Hejazi says its use in drinks and desserts is still "an emerging trend" and hasn't yet hit the mainstream in the UK.

So, is it translating to real-life demand?

We're not yet seeing sweetcorn milk stocked in supermarkets and corn lattes at mainstream coffee chains.

But Natalie TJ, who co-runs an Asian-inspired bakery in London, says her cornmilk matcha drink has been one of the most popular drinks this summer – second only to the bakery's Hong Kong milk tea.

"Many coffee shops in Asia sell corn milk matcha," she says, adding that customers have probably been seeking out the drink at the cafe as it is not as common as other matcha combinations in the UK.

Other UK bakeries and dessert shops have been featuring sweetcorn baked goods on their menus too.

Pophams bakery, which has branches in east London, has had a peach and sweetcorn danish pastry on its menu.

"Our customers were very intrigued by the flavour combination, and once they tried it, they were pleasantly surprised by how well the flavours worked together," said Ollie Gold, the bakery's founder.

Elsewhere, chain gelato brand Snowflake makes a sweetcorn-flavoured "Snow Cob", while more mainstream, high-end supermarkets and chocolate brands are selling corn kernels covered in chocolate.

But part-time baker Supreedha Iyer says there is still some confusion among her friends when she presents them with her own sweetcorn-flavoured bakes.

Iyer, who grew up in Malaysia but now lives in London, recently made a version of maritozzi buns – a brioche filled with cream - using sweetcorn, inspired by a bun she ate as a child.

"My Asian friends immediately understood the flavour, while my British friends were much more confused about whether it was supposed to be sweet or savoury," she says. "There was genuine confusion!"

"That does seem to be changing though," she adds. "British bakers are beginning to explore corn more confidently".

articles.title: Serious questions over use of UK emergency alerts, its creators say
articles.summary: Millions across England and Wales received a wildfire alert on their phones earlier this month, but it partly backfired.
articles.body:
As the Conservative minister who launched the UK's emergency alert system, Oliver Dowden was more than familiar with the loud bleeping sound coming from his phone earlier this month.

What took him by a surprise was the message on the screen.

Like millions of people across England and Wales, the "severe alert" on 14 August warned him of a "very high risk of wildfires nationally" and against doing anything that could start a fire, including lighting disposable barbecues.

It was the biggest use of the system to date - but Dowden has now weighed in to question whether it was strictly necessary.

Dowden and two officials who helped create the government's emergency alert system are calling for Labour ministers to be up front with the public on what it could be used for in future.

"I was surprised at the decision to issue this nationwide alert and it raises some serious questions," Dowden, who served as deputy prime minister under Rishi Sunak, tells BBC News.

"The government needs to clarify the criteria for its use and why this alert met those criteria."

When he fronted the launch of the alert system in April 2023, he says it was intended for as narrow a geographic area as possible where the threat to life is imminent.

The government's own webpage for emergency alerts says they are only sent for "life-threatening emergencies", listing wildfires, severe flooding and extreme storms.

Two national tests of the system took place in 2023 and 2025, while 10 local alerts have been sent since its launch, all related to weather or flooding bar one in Plymouth for a World War Two bomb removal.

The day before the alert was sent earlier this month, 19 homes burned down in the west Midlands town of Stourbridge after a wildfire. The day of the alert, ministers say they were asked directly by fire chiefs to send one as crews dealt with 43 wildfires and 11 major incidents across the country.

The government's Cobra emergency committee met to discuss how to respond. After sign off from Prime Minister Andy Burnham's de facto deputy Louise Haigh, the alert was sent at 19:00 on 14 August.

It triggered a backlash on social media with some vowing to opt out of further alerts in their phone settings, domestic abuse charities and survivors saying victims with hidden phones were put at risk , and confusion about alerts sent multiple times.

Dowden's worry is that the wildfire alert was more like a public information campaign than an imminent threat to life across all of England and Wales.

"People need to know that when they receive an alert, it is a genuine imminent emergency," the Conservative MP says. "If that confidence is lost, people will simply ignore it."

A Cabinet Office report during trials in 2014 warned of this "cry wolf" effect, while pointing out there was strong support among the public for the alerts.

"Alerts should not be issued just because the government wants to be seen to be doing something," Dowden adds.

The National Fire Chiefs Council said the alert heightened people's awareness and public behaviour, while government insiders point out wildfire alerts are commonplace in many European countries.

"By following the guidance that was issued, people were able to take the necessary steps to keep themselves safe and front line services recorded a significant decrease in incidents in the following days," a government spokesperson said.

But Frazer Rhodes, who worked in government across a decade to help build the technology and devise high thresholds for the alerts, feels a review is now necessary to avoid future ones backfiring.

He was in a bar in Halifax, West Yorkshire, with his wife when the sound of pinging phones began echoing around.

"Everybody around was just going, 'what's this?' What's this?'" he tells us. "Then my wife shouted, 'he did that'."

His wife's joke aside, he said his "immediate thought" was whether it met the threshold for sending one. He explains: "At its heart are three criteria: urgency, severity and certainty. So, in simple terms, how bad, how soon, and how sure?"

Rhodes thinks the wildfire alert arguably met the bar for urgency and severity, but perhaps not for certainty of a threat to life.

"It should be very rare to get an alert," he points out.

He thinks ministers should accept there has been a divided response and launch a review to ask themselves: "How do we do this differently?"

Rhodes, a service delivery specialist, adds: "The national protocol should be a public document… I think that document is almost like a contract with us to say 'this is when we're going to use it, these are the perameters, this is who can use it'."

The emergency alerts we may get in future

Back in 2021 when designing the alerts, he says these were the scenarios considered valid for future alerts:

Severe weather and environmental alerts such as flood risk

Major hazards such as the Buncefield oil depot fire in 2005

When building the UK alert system, which cost up to £25.3m in its first three years, officials looked to Australia and New Zealand where emergency alerts have no "opt out" option for the public, unlike in the UK. They also considered minor types of public safety alerts which are sent in the US for issues such as missing children.

The alert targets individual cell towers with a radiowave-like signal, allowing all mobile phones in the area to pick it up without needing to know people's mobile numbers. This cell broadcast technology is used instead of SMS texts or an app.

It comes as the Cabinet Office plans to launch a separate campaign in the autumn about how people can make themselves and their homes more prepared for extreme weather and cyber-attacks.

Another one of those involved in creating the alert system, Nick Corney, thinks the government "missed a trick" with the wildfire alert by sending it nationally rather than targeted at specific postcodes with the highest risk.

Corney, who worked in the Cabinet Office between 2018 and 2021 and says he was in weekly and then daily meetings about designing alerts, wants a "thorough review".

He says this would look at making future alert wording more specific, such as explaining the threat to life with a link to a webpage. "An extra level of consideration needs to be put in place" for national alert versus a local one, he adds.

"You've really got to take yourself out of the Cobra room," he says.

"There's a level of scaring the public that needs to be taken into consideration."
